title: Privacy and Copyright Protection in Generative AI: A Lifecycle Perspective
venue: 2024 IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering - Software Engineering for AI (CAIN)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of privacy and copyright risks created by Generative AI systems trained on large-scale data. The authors argue that existing approaches such as differential privacy, machine unlearning, and data poisoning address only isolated parts of the problem, rather than the full lifecycle of data used in GenAI systems.

The paper proposes a lifecycle perspective for organizing privacy and copyright protections across stages including problem formulation, data collection, data cleaning, annotation, model training, evaluation, deployment, inference, and data distribution. It identifies recurring challenges at each stage, including consent and license acquisition, transparency and data access, consent modification and withdrawal, provenance and attribution, side effects of protection mechanisms, continuous monitoring for breaches and violations, and downstream distribution of outputs.

Rather than reporting an empirical study, the paper offers a conceptual framework and research agenda. It recommends lifecycle-wide safeguards such as consent management, machine forgetting, privacy/copyright guardrails, and an AI Bill of Materials that records consent and license information. The main conclusion is that privacy and copyright protection in GenAI require integrated, end-to-end solutions grounded in the data lifecycle, not ad hoc point fixes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/lifecycle framework paper on privacy and copyright in generative AI, not an empirical study of educational intervention effects. It does not report a study design, sample, or causal evaluation relevant to K-12 outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact and does not evaluate any intervention in classrooms or learning settings. Its contribution is conceptual and legal/technical rather than outcome-based.
